en.t: Why do the least skilled people feel the most confident?
In 1999, two psychologists ran a simple experiment.
They tested people's skill, then asked them to guess their own score.

fa: سال ۱۹۹۹ دو روان‌شناس یک آزمایش ساده اجرا کردند
مهارت آدم‌ها را سنجیدند، بعد خواستند نمره‌ی خودشان را حدس بزنند

en.t: The bottom quarter scored around the twelfth percentile.

fa: نمره‌ی واقعی چارک پایین: صدک دوازدهم
حدس خودشان از نمره‌شان؟ صدک شصت‌وهشتم

en.t: They lacked the very skill needed to see the skill.

fa: این اعتمادبه‌نفس نیست؛ خطای خودپنداره است
آن‌ها همان مهارتی را نداشتند که برای دیدن مهارت لازم است

en.t: Meanwhile the top scorers rated themselves just average,

fa: اما برترین‌ها خودشان را فقط متوسط ارزیابی کردند

en.t: because they assumed everyone else found it easy too.

fa: چون فرض کردند بقیه هم همین‌قدر راحت پیدا کرده‌اند

en.t: The cure is the loop: test yourself, compare, update.
Skill grows together with the watcher.

fa: درمان همان حلقه است: خودآزمایی، مقایسه، به‌روزرسانی
مهارت همراه با ناظر رشد می‌کند

en.t: This is metacognition HQ: training the watcher in your head.

fa: اینجا metacognition HQ است: ستاد تربیت ناظرِ داخل سرت

en.t: Follow along, and check your calibration in the next quiz.

fa: فالو کن و در کوییز بعدی کالیبراسیون خودت را بسنج

caption.hook: Why do the least skilled people feel the most confident?
caption.intro: In 1999, Kruger & Dunning put it in numbers: people in the bottom quarter of a skill rated themselves around the 68th percentile. Not lies. Not ego. A metacognition gap — the same skill that makes you good is the skill that lets you SEE that you're good.

sections.title: WHY IT HAPPENS
lines: Double burden: low skill means poor answers AND poor monitoring
The curve bends: experts slightly underestimate themselves
Noticing the gap is the first rep of the watcher

sources: Kruger & Dunning (1999), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1121-1134
Dunning (2011), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 44
Fleming & Lau (2014), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 8
